definition: A substance made of only one element or compound, not mixed with anything else. Has a fixed, sharp melting and boiling point.
Two or more substances combined but not chemically bonded. Components can be separated by physical methods and have a range of melting/boiling points.
A mixture that has been designed and made to have specific, useful properties. Examples include medicines, alloys, fuels, fertilisers, and cosmetics.
A technique used to separate and identify the components of a mixture. Components separate because they have different solubilities in the solvent and different attractions to the stationary phase.
The phase that does not move in chromatography. In paper chromatography, this is the paper. Substances with greater attraction to the stationary phase move less.
The phase that moves in chromatography, carrying the substances with it. In paper chromatography, this is the solvent.
A value used to identify substances in chromatography. Calculated as: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.
Another name for Rf value — the ratio of the distance moved by a substance to the distance moved by the solvent front.
A chromatography technique that uses a gas as the mobile phase to separate and identify substances in a mixture. Can be linked to mass spectrometry for identification.
A test used to identify metal ions in a compound by observing the colour of the flame when the compound is burned. Different metals produce characteristic colours.
A test in which two solutions are mixed and an insoluble precipitate forms if a particular ion is present. Used to identify metal ions and halide ions.
A test for metal ions: adding NaOH solution to a metal salt solution produces a coloured precipitate if certain metal ions are present (e.g. blue for Cu²⁺, green for Fe²⁺, brown for Fe³⁺).
A test for halide ions: adding silver nitrate solution (acidified with dilute nitric acid) produces a precipitate whose colour identifies the halide — white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), yellow (I⁻).
A test for sulfate ions (SO₄²⁻): adding acidified barium chloride solution produces a white precipitate of barium sulfate if sulfate ions are present.
A test for carbonate ions: adding dilute acid produces carbon dioxide gas, which turns limewater milky.
A test for carbon dioxide gas: CO₂ turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) from colourless to milky/cloudy white.
A technique that identifies metal ions by analysing the wavelengths of light emitted when a sample is placed in a flame. More accurate and sensitive than a simple flame test.
A test for purity: a pure substance has a sharp, specific melting point. An impure substance melts over a range of temperatures and at a lower temperature than the pure substance.
A test using litmus paper or solution to determine whether a substance is acidic (turns red) or alkaline (turns blue). Does not give a precise pH.
A test for ammonium ions (NH₄⁺): adding NaOH solution and heating produces ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.
